claim: Propranolol is an approved non-selective β-adrenergic blocker that is first line therapy for infantile hemangioma.
source: Propranolol is an approved non-selective β-adrenergic blocker that is first line therapy for infantile hemangioma.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about propranolol's approved use and mechanism.

claim: Human mutations in the SOX18 gene give rise to Hypotrichosis-Lymphedema-Telangiectasia and Renal syndrome (HLTRS).
source: Human mutations in the SOX18 gene give rise to Hypotrichosis-Lymphedema-Telangiectasia and Renal syndrome (HLTRS) (Irrthum et al., 2003; Moalem et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research establishing this genetic relationship.

claim: Most disease-causing SOX18 mutations lead to a premature truncation at the C-terminus due to an early stop codon.
source: Most disease-causing SOX18 mutations lead to a premature truncation at the C-terminus due to an early stop codon, producing defective protein products that act in a dominant negative fashion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the nature of SOX18 mutations in HLTRS.

claim: The mutated SOX18 protein can still bind to chromatin but fails to recruit its protein partner(s) to transactivate target genes.
source: The mutated SOX18 protein can still bind to chromatin but fails to recruit its protein partner(s) to transactivate target genes, and thereby disrupts the endogenous function of SOX18.
evidence: This describes the molecular mechanism of the dominant-negative mutation based on established understanding.

claim: The dominant-negative mutant prevents other SOX transcription factors to act redundantly and rescue the molecular pathway.
source: Further, the dominant-negative mutant prevents other SOX transcription factors to act redundantly and rescue the molecular pathway (Hosking et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: From birth to adolescence HLTRS patients develop symptoms such as lymphedema and abnormalities to hair and nails for which very limited effective treatment options exist.
source: From birth to adolescence HLTRS patients develop symptoms such as lymphedema and abnormalities to hair and nails for which very limited effective treatment options exist.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about HLTRS presentation and treatment options.

claim: A recent HLTRS patient had symptoms so mild that the initial diagnosis failed to identify this syndrome, mostly due to the absence of lymphedema up until late adolescence.
source: A recent report of an HLTRS patient described symptoms so mild that the initial diagnosis failed to identify this syndrome, mostly due to the absence of lymphedema up until late adolescence (Wünnemann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to a case report.

claim: Whole-exome sequencing led to the discovery of a premature stop-codon in SOX18, p.Q161*, in an HLTRS patient.
source: Eventually, the patient was subjected to whole-exome sequencing, which led to the discovery of a premature stop-codon in SOX18, p.Q161*; with such a mutation the patient would be expected to present a severe phenotype.
evidence: Supported by citation to a case report describing this patient.

claim: The HLTRS patient with p.Q161* mutation had been treated with high doses propranolol since a young age due to a significant dilation of the thoracic artery causing a high blood pressure.
source: A search for a potential cause of the milder course of the syndrome in this patient revealed that she had been treated with high doses propranolol since a young age due to a significant dilation of the thoracic artery causing a high blood pressure.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from a case report.

claim: The milder phenotype observed in this HLTRS patient coincident with the course of the propranolol treatment raised the possibility that this drug has a SOX18-dependent molecular mode of action in addition to its β-blocking activity.
source: The milder phenotype observed in this HLTRS patient coincident with the course of the propranolol treatment raised the possibility that this drug has a SOX18-dependent molecular mode of action in addition to its β-blocking activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the clinical observation.

claim: The main indications for propranolol therapy are hypertension, ischemic heart disease, arrhythmia, migraine and essential tremor.
source: The main indications for propranolol therapy are hypertension, ischemic heart disease, arrhythmia, migraine and essential tremor.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about propranolol's clinical uses.

claim: Sensitivity to propranolol does not always correlate with the expression levels of the β-adrenergic receptors.
source: Sensitivity to propranolol does not always correlate with the expression levels of the β-adrenergic receptors (Wolter et al., 2014; MacDonald et al., 2006; Chang et al., 2015; Powe et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Propranolol use in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy revealed its beneficial effects in infantile hemangioma.
source: Propranolol use in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy revealed its beneficial effects in infantile hemangioma (Léauté-Labrèze et al., 2008), raising the possibility that β-adrenergic receptor signaling, and thus by inference, propranolol, modulates VEGF levels (Chen et al., 2013; Ozeki et al., 2013; Lavine et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Propranolol is a racemic mixture with R(+) and S(-) enantiomers in equal proportions.
source: Further, this drug is a racemic mixture with R(+) and S(-) enantiomers in equal proportions.
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge about propranolol's composition.

claim: The S(-) form displays most of the anti-β-adrenergic activity, whereas the R(+) enantiomer is carried over during drug synthesis.
source: The S(-) form displays most of the anti-β-adrenergic activity, whereas the R(+) enantiomer is carried over during drug synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the differential activity of propranolol enantiomers.

claim: An HLTRS patient diagnosed at 11 months of age had a truncation mutation in SOX18 (SOX18 c.492_505dup).
source: The patient was diagnosed with HLTRS at 11 months of age, after presenting with alopecia, edema and telangiectasia (Bastaki et al., 2016). Exome sequencing revealed that this patient had a truncation mutation in SOX18 (SOX18 c.492_505dup).
evidence: Supported by citation to a case report.

claim: In September 2015, at 17 months of age, the HLTRS patient developed progressive pericardial effusion over 3 weeks, which required pericardiocentesis.
source: In September 2015, at 17 months of age, he developed progressive pericardial effusion over 3 weeks, which required pericardiocentesis.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the case report.

claim: Two weeks after the pericardiocentesis procedure, pericardial effusion re-accumulated progressively over 6 weeks, despite strong anti-inflammatory regimens including 3 weeks of oral ibuprofen and 10 days of oral prednisone.
source: Two weeks after the procedure, pericardial effusion re-accumulated progressively over 6 weeks, despite strong anti-inflammatory regimens including 3 weeks of oral ibuprofen and 10 days of oral prednisone.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the case report.

claim: Oral propranolol was introduced and increased gradually every 2–3 weeks from 0.8 mg/kg/day in three divided doses to reach a maximum of 4.1 mg/kg/day in the HLTRS patient.
source: After obtaining parental consent, oral propranolol was introduced and increased gradually every 2–3 weeks from 0.8 mg/kg/day in three divided doses to reach a maximum of 4.1 mg/kg/day, as tolerated clinically (pulmonary wheezing).
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the case report.

claim: Spontaneous and rapid resolution of the pericardial effusion was observed after reaching a dose threshold of 3 mg/kg/day propranolol.
source: We observed spontaneous and rapid resolution of the pericardial effusion after reaching a dose threshold of 3 mg/kg/day.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the case report.

claim: Propranolol treatment resulted in significant reduction in pericardial effusion which did not recur as of June 2018.
source: Echocardiography revealed that pericardiocentesis was not required anymore after propranolol treatment due to significant reduction in pericardial effusion (pink arrow) which did not recur as of June 2018 (time of the study).
evidence: This is supported by clinical data and echocardiography images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Propranolol affected the survival of fetal endothelial colony forming cells (ECFC) at equivalent doses whereas Atenolol (specific β1 blocker) and ICI118,551 (specific β2) did not.
source: Propranolol affected the survival of ECFC at equivalent doses whereas Atenolol (specific β1 blocker) and ICI118,551 (specific β2) did not.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of specific β-adrenergic receptors did not replicate the marked effect propranolol had in the ECFC survival assay.
source: Results showed that pharmacological inhibition of specific β-adrenergic receptors did not replicate the marked effect propranolol had in the ECFC survival assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The cytotoxic activity of propranolol was unaltered when ADRB2 was silenced in ISO-HAS angiosarcoma cells.
source: The cytotoxic activity of propranolol (Figure 1D) and its enhancement of vinblastine cytotoxicity (Figure 1E) were unaltered when ADRB2 was silenced.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The enhancement of vinblastine cytotoxicity by propranolol was unaltered when ADRB2 was silenced in ISO-HAS angiosarcoma cells.
source: The cytotoxic activity of propranolol (Figure 1D) and its enhancement of vinblastine cytotoxicity (Figure 1E) were unaltered when ADRB2 was silenced.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The anti-survival and sensitization to chemotherapy activities of propranolol are independent of β-adrenergic receptor expression.
source: These results show that the anti-survival and sensitization to chemotherapy activities of propranolol are independent of β-adrenergic receptor expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of ADRB2 knockdown.

claim: Knock-down of ADRB1 and ADRB2 alone or in combination did not affect the ability of propranolol to block the proliferative response in SHEP neuroblastoma cell line.
source: Similar results were obtained when using a non-endothelial cell type (SHEP neuroblastoma cell line) whereby knock-down of ADRB1 and ADRB2 alone or in combination did not affect the ability of propranolol to block the proliferative response and its ability to enhance response to chemo-therapies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Knock-down of ADRB1 and ADRB2 alone or in combination did not affect the ability of propranolol to enhance response to chemo-therapies in SHEP neuroblastoma cell line.
source: Similar results were obtained when using a non-endothelial cell type (SHEP neuroblastoma cell line) whereby knock-down of ADRB1 and ADRB2 alone or in combination did not affect the ability of propranolol to block the proliferative response and its ability to enhance response to chemo-therapies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SOX18 Ragged Opossum (RaOp) mouse mutant is considered a murine counterpart of human HLTRS syndrome.
source: This mouse mutant is considered a murine counterpart of human HLTRS syndrome since it displays the same range of cardio-vascular and hair follicle defects and exhibits the same type of dominant-negative mutation in the Sox18 gene (Pennisi et al., 2000; Downes et al., 2009; François et al., 2008; Villani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The Ragged mouse is characterized by pathologic corneal neo-vascularisation (CNV).
source: The Ragged mouse is characterized by pathologic corneal neo-vascularisation (CNV, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C) (François and Ramchandran, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation and images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Treatment with propranolol (21 days) did not affect the gross morphological appearance of either wild type or RaOp pups.
source: Treatment with propranolol (21 days) did not affect the gross morphological appearance of either wild type or RaOp pups, nor did it significantly affect the weight of the RaOp animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B, n = 5–10 mice per group).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Treatment with propranolol (21 days) did not significantly affect the weight of the RaOp animals.
source: Treatment with propranolol (21 days) did not affect the gross morphological appearance of either wild type or RaOp pups, nor did it significantly affect the weight of the RaOp animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B, n = 5–10 mice per group).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: No obvious side effects were observed from propranolol treatment in RaOp mice, consistent with the safety profile of propranolol established over the past decades.
source: We did not observe any obvious side effects, consistent with the safety profile of propranolol established over the past decades.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and established knowledge about propranolol safety.

claim: Propranolol treatment of RaOp mice led to an almost complete rescue of the CNV phenotype.
source: Propranolol treatment of RaOp mice, however, led to an almost complete rescue of the CNV phenotype (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The corneas from propranolol-treated mutant animals were devoid of blood vessels in five out of five mice, and one mutant pup only had a mild penetration of blood vessels into the cornea.
source: The corneas from propranolol-treated mutant animals were devoid of blood vessels (Figure 2A, Endomucin- and ERG-positive cells) in five out of five mice, and one mutant pup only had a mild penetration of blood vessels into the cornea (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Propranolol treatment is an effective therapeutic strategy to block aberrant vessel growth in a mouse model of HLTRS.
source: These pre-clinical data indicate that propranolol treatment is an effective therapeutic strategy to block aberrant vessel growth in a mouse model of HLTRS and is indicative of on-target engagement on SOX18 protein in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing rescue of CNV phenotype.

claim: RaOp behaves in a dominant negative fashion and is capable to inhibit SOX18 WT function even at low 30:1 (w/w DNA) allelic ratios.
source: RaOp behaves in a dominant negative fashion and is capable to inhibit SOX18 WT function even at low 30:1 (w/w DNA) allelic ratios.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of propranolol to the media rescues SOX18 dependent activity of the Vcam1 promoter in presence of RaOp.
source: Addition of propranolol to the media rescues SOX18 dependent activity of the Vcam1 promoter in presence of RaOp.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The effect of propranolol on SOX18 activity is concentration dependent and normal SOX18 activity on the Vcam1 construct is achieved at 15 µM propranolol.
source: Effect is concentration dependent and normal SOX18 activity on this construct is achieved at 15 µM propranolol.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Propranolol is a small compound with the ability to disrupt SOX18 self-recruitment.
source: Propranolol is a small compound with the ability to disrupt SOX18 self-recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Propranolol showed a mild efficacy at disrupting SOX18 homodimer.
source: Propranolol showed a mild efficacy at disrupting SOX18 homodimer and was able to interfere more effectively with the assembly of the non functional SOX18/RaOp protein complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ALPHAScreen assay.

claim: Propranolol was able to interfere more effectively with the assembly of the non functional SOX18/RaOp protein complex.
source: Propranolol showed a mild efficacy at disrupting SOX18 homodimer and was able to interfere more effectively with the assembly of the non functional SOX18/RaOp protein complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ALPHAScreen assay.

claim: RBPJ was recently shown to act as a SOX18 protein partner.
source: An effector of the NOTCH signaling pathway (RBPJ) was recently shown to act as a SOX18 protein partner (Overman et al., 2017; Fontaine et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Propranolol inhibits the association of SOX18 with RBPJ at low micro-molar range (5 μM).
source: In addition to disrupting SOX18 homodimer assembly (Figure 2C), we found that propranolol inhibits the association of SOX18 with RBPJ at low micro-molar range (5 μM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: When using Sm4 as a reference, propranolol was equally effective at disrupting SOX18/RBPJ PPI however not as effective at blocking SOX18 homodimer formation.
source: When using Sm4 as a reference, propranolol was equally effective at disrupting SOX18/RBPJ PPI however not as effective at blocking SOX18 homodimer formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The same molecular mode of action of propranolol accounts for both the rescue of dominant-negative SOX18 loss of function by disruption of the non-functional SOX18/RaOp (Q161*) complex, and the disruption of functional SOX18 wild type PPIs.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the same molecular mode of action of propranolol accounts for both the rescue of dominant-negative SOX18 loss of function by disruption of the non-functional SOX18/RaOp (Q161*) complex, and the disruption of functional SOX18 wild type PPIs, namely SOX18/RBPJ and SOX18/SOX18 dimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on protein-protein interactions.

claim: Propranolol is the mainstay of treatment for infantile hemangioma.
source: Although the molecular mode of action of propranolol in infantile hemangioma therapy is largely unknown, it is the mainstay of treatment for infantile hemangioma. (Léauté-Labrèze et al., 2008; Léauté-Labrèze et al., 2015a; Léauté-Labrèze et al., 2015b)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A variety of propranolol-induced cellular effects have been observed in infantile hemangioma-derived stem cells (HemSCs), hemangioma endothelial cells (HemECs) and hemangioma pericytes.
source: A variety of propranolol-induced cellular effects have been observed in infantile hemangioma-derived stem cells (HemSCs), hemangioma endothelial cells (HemECs) and hemangioma pericytes (Lamy et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2014; Tu et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SOX18 protein was observed in a sup-population of CD31-positive endothelial cells in hemangioma tissue sections from three patients.
source: SOX18 protein was observed in a sup-population of CD31-positive endothelial cells (Figure 3A, arrows) and SOX18 mRNA was expressed in ECFC (positive control) and in HemEC, whereas HemSC showed low expression and hemangioma pericytes were completely devoid of SOX18 transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SOX18 mRNA was expressed in ECFC (positive control) and in HemEC, whereas HemSC showed low expression and hemangioma pericytes were completely devoid of SOX18 transcripts.
source: SOX18 protein was observed in a sup-population of CD31-positive endothelial cells (Figure 3A, arrows) and SOX18 mRNA was expressed in ECFC (positive control) and in HemEC, whereas HemSC showed low expression and hemangioma pericytes were completely devoid of SOX18 transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: VEGF-B treatment of HemSC from four different infantile hemangiomas resulted in increased CDH5, SOX18 and ADBR2 mRNA.
source: VEGF-B treatment of HemSC from four different infantile hemangiomas resulted in increased CDH5 (an endothelial cell marker), SOX18 and ADBR2 (β2 adrenergic receptor) mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: VEGF-B treatment of HemSC resulted in increased CD31, NOTCH1, PLXND1 and VEGFR1 expression.
source: This was extended to other genes such as CD31, NOTCH1, PLXND1 and VEGFR1 (Table 1 and Figure 3—source data 1), each of which are expressed in infantile hemangioma endothelium in vivo (Boscolo et al., 2011; Nakayama et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2010), further confirming the successful differentiation of HemSCs into HemECs (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Propranolol significantly decreased VEGF-B induced expression of all five endothelial markers in HemSC to levels also achieved by Sm4 as compared to controls.
source: Propranolol significantly decreased VEGF-B induced expression of all five endothelial markers in HemSC to levels also achieved by Sm4 as compared to controls (see p-values in Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and source data.

claim: The S(-) form displays potent anti-β-adrenergic activity whereas the R(+) enantiomer presents strongly reduced antagonist activity towards β2 adrenergic receptors on peripheral arteries.
source: The S(-) form displays potent anti-β-adrenergic activity whereas the R(+) enantiomer presents strongly reduced antagonist activity towards β2 adrenergic receptors on peripheral arteries (Stoschitzky et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The R(+) enantiomer recapitulated propranolol and Sm4-induced inhibition on all markers in HemSC to HemEC differentiation assay.
source: The R(+) enantiomer recapitulated propranolol and Sm4-induced inhibition on all markers, whereas the S(-) enantiomer showed only weak or no inhibition on hemangioma markers (Figure 3D and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The S(-) enantiomer showed only weak or no inhibition on hemangioma markers in HemSC to HemEC differentiation assay.
source: The R(+) enantiomer recapitulated propranolol and Sm4-induced inhibition on all markers, whereas the S(-) enantiomer showed only weak or no inhibition on hemangioma markers (Figure 3D and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: These results are consistent with a SOX18-dependent, β-adrenergic receptor independent blockade of hemangioma endothelial differentiation.
source: These results are consistent with a SOX18-dependent, β-adrenergic receptor independent blockade of hemangioma endothelial differentiation, which strongly suggests that blockade of SOX18 activity is the main mode of action of propranolol in this setting.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential activity of the enantiomers.

claim: Analysis of VEGF-R2 expression and phosphorylation levels in ECFC and HemSC to EC differentiation assay ruled out that the propranolol racemic mixture, the R(+) enantiomer or Sm4 interfere with the VEGF signaling pathway.
source: Further, analysis of VEGF-R2 expression and phosphorylation levels in ECFC and HemSC to EC differentiation assay ruled out that the propranolol racemic mixture, the R(+) enantiomer or Sm4 interfere with the VEGF signaling pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: Both propranolol and the R(+) enantiomer prevented aberrant vessel growth in the corneal tissue of the heterozygous mutant animals.
source: In this in vivo setting both propranolol and the R(+) enantiomer prevented aberrant vessel growth in the corneal tissue of the heterozygous mutant animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The S(-) enantiomer was also active at disrupting corneal vessel outgrowth.
source: Of note the S(-) enantiomer was also active at disrupting corneal vessel outgrowth, suggesting that conformational changes that occur in the SOX18 mutated protein may attenuate the discrepancy in enantiomeric activities previously observed in the hemangioma endothelial differentiation model (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The RaOp mouse presented with a highly disorganized lymphatic vascular network.
source: As previously reported the RaOp mouse presented with a highly disorganized lymphatic vascular network (François et al., 2008) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, top graph).
evidence: Supported by citation and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Neither the propranolol racemic mixture nor its enantiomers rescued the lymphatic vascular phenotype caused by the RaOp mutation in the skin.
source: In the skin, neither the propranolol racemic mixture nor its enantiomers rescued the lymphatic vascular phenotype caused by the RaOp mutation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4); this is most likely due to the post-natal timing of the treatment: lymphatic vascular defects are acquired in the RaOp mutant during the initial steps of embryonic lymphangiogenesis (early to mid-organogenesis), which precedes the drug treatment window.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Lymphatic vascular defects are acquired in the RaOp mutant during the initial steps of embryonic lymphangiogenesis (early to mid-organogenesis), which precedes the drug treatment window.
source: In the skin, neither the propranolol racemic mixture nor its enantiomers rescued the lymphatic vascular phenotype caused by the RaOp mutation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4); this is most likely due to the post-natal timing of the treatment: lymphatic vascular defects are acquired in the RaOp mutant during the initial steps of embryonic lymphangiogenesis (early to mid-organogenesis), which precedes the drug treatment window.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of treatment and known developmental biology.

claim: The R(+) enantiomer of propranolol is a potent selective inhibitor of SOX18 activity.
source: In summary, we suggest the R(+) enantiomer of propranolol is a potent selective inhibitor of SOX18 activity and it is sufficient to achieve the effects of propranolol racemic mixture in the context of infantile hemangioma and other SOX18-dependent vascular diseases.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing R(+) enantiomer activity.

claim: The R(+) enantiomer is sufficient to achieve the effects of propranolol racemic mixture in the context of infantile hemangioma and other SOX18-dependent vascular diseases.
source: In summary, we suggest the R(+) enantiomer of propranolol is a potent selective inhibitor of SOX18 activity and it is sufficient to achieve the effects of propranolol racemic mixture in the context of infantile hemangioma and other SOX18-dependent vascular diseases.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing R(+) enantiomer activity.

claim: Approximately 20% of the patient population fails to respond to propranolol treatment and/or experience tumor regrowth when the medication is discontinued too early.
source: Despite being the front line therapy for infantile hemangioma, approximately 20% of the patient population fails to respond to propranolol treatment and/or experience tumor regrowth when the medication is discontinued too early (Bagazgoitia et al., 2011; Xiao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clinical trials of the R(+) versus the S(-) form have been performed and deemed safe with full toxicology data available.
source: Clinical trials of the R(+) versus the S(-) form have been performed and deemed safe with full toxicology data available (Stensrud and Sjaastad, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Pharmacokinetic studies suggest that propranolol therapy results in an accumulation of the S(-) enantiomer following drug metabolism.
source: Pharmacokinetic studies suggest that propranolol therapy results in an accumulation of the S(-) enantiomer following drug metabolism, which could be problematic if one is interested in the activity of the R(+) form (Mehvar and Brocks, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Toxicology studies suggest that propranolol in its racemic form is more toxic than either enantiomer alone.
source: Indeed toxicology studies further suggest that propranolol in its racemic form is more toxic than either enantiomer alone (Stoschitzky et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The observation that the S(-) enantiomer also has the capability to rescue the corneal neo-vascularisation phenotype in a pre-clinical model of HTLRS suggests that the effects of propranolol as a racemic mixture are likely to be a combination of the blockade of beta-adrenergic receptor activity and SOX18 RaOp mutant protein inhibition.
source: The observation that the S(-) enantiomer also has the capability to rescue the corneal neo-vascularisation phenotype in a pre-clinical model of HTLRS suggests that the effects of propranolol as a racemic mixture are likely to be a combination of the blockade of beta-adrenergic receptor activity and SOX18 RaOp mutant protein inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing S(-) enantiomer activity in the RaOp model.

claim: The SOX18 wild type protein blockade displays some enantio-selectivity, whereas conformational changes in the SOX18/RaOp complex caused by the RaOp mutation sensitize the dominant-negative protein complex to both R(+) and S(-) enantiomers.
source: This may suggest that the SOX18 wild type protein blockade displays some enantio-selectivity, whereas conformational changes in the SOX18/RaOp complex caused by the RaOp mutation sensitize the dominant-negative protein complex to both R(+) and S(-) enantiomers.
evidence: This is speculated based on the differential activity of enantiomers in different models.

claim: There may be critical time windows in which treatment with R(+) propranolol would be most efficient as an anti-angiogenic compound via a blockade of SOX18 transcriptional activity.
source: The studies in human patients with HLTRS and the murine RaOP model suggest that there may be critical time windows in which treatment with R(+) propranolol would be most efficient as an anti-angiogenic compound via a blockade of SOX18 transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the timing-dependent effects observed in different vascular beds.

claim: The low number of patients with HLTRS makes it difficult to establish genotype-phenotype relationships in greater detail.
source: The low number of patients with HLTRS – less than 10 documented survivors have been reported – makes it difficult to establish genotype-phenotype relationships in greater detail.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the rarity of HLTRS.

claim: The R(+) enantiomer is a SOX18 small molecule inhibitor with weak anti-beta adrenergic activity whereas the S(-) molecule is both a beta-blocker and a weak SOX18 inhibitor.
source: Our findings outline that the R(+) enantiomer is a SOX18 small molecule inhibitor with weak anti-beta adrenergic activity whereas the S(-) molecule is both a beta-blocker and a weak SOX18 inhibitor which introduces variability in net efficacy of propranolol treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on enantiomer activities.

claim: R-propranolol is a small molecule inhibitor of the SOX18 transcription factor.
source: Dissection of the molecular mechanism identified the R(+)-propranolol enantiomer as a small molecule inhibitor of the SOX18 transcription factor, independent of any anti-adrenergic effect.
evidence: This is the main finding supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: R(+)-propranolol acts as a small molecule inhibitor of SOX18 independent of any anti-adrenergic effect.
source: Dissection of the molecular mechanism identified the R(+)-propranolol enantiomer as a small molecule inhibitor of the SOX18 transcription factor, independent of any anti-adrenergic effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing activity independent of beta-adrenergic receptors.

claim: Propranolol treatment rescues corneal neo-vascularisation phenotype in a mouse pre-clinical model of HLTRS.
source: Using a mouse pre-clinical model of HLTRS, we show that propranolol treatment rescues its corneal neo-vascularisation phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Propranolol successfully treated pericardial edema in a patient with HLTRS syndrome caused by a mutation in SOX18.
source: Here, we report successful treatment of pericardial edema with propranolol in a patient with Hypotrichosis-Lymphedema-Telangiectasia and Renal (HLTRS) syndrome, caused by a mutation in SOX18.
evidence: This is supported by clinical data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: SOX18 has an etiological role in vascular neoplasms.
source: Our work emphasizes the importance of SOX18 etiological role in vascular neoplasms, and suggests R(+)-propranolol repurposing to numerous indications ranging from vascular diseases to metastatic cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing SOX18 involvement in hemangioma and vascular diseases.

claim: R(+)-propranolol has therapeutic potential for repurposing to numerous indications ranging from vascular diseases to metastatic cancer.
source: Our work emphasizes the importance of SOX18 etiological role in vascular neoplasms, and suggests R(+)-propranolol repurposing to numerous indications ranging from vascular diseases to metastatic cancer.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings about R(+)-propranolol's mechanism of action.
